title: I am: the self's first words
hookLine: before anything else exists, the self says its first words, then feels its first fear, then its first loneliness
carry: i am, before the ego adds a name
tomorrow: the self split in two — husband and wife, the whole world

cards: A knock on a door. Someone inside calls: who is it? And the answer often comes before any name: it's me.
A small habit, easy to miss. The Brihadaranyaka stops to explain it, in the middle of telling how the world began.
That habit, it says, goes all the way back to the first moment there was anyone at all: the first words ever spoken, and the two feelings that came right after them.

teach.b: In the beginning, the text says, there was only the self, in the shape of a person. It looked around and saw nothing but itself. And the first thing it said was aham asmi.
I am. So it came to be called I. That's why, the text adds, when anyone is called even now, they first say it's me, and then whatever other name they have.
Then the self was afraid. That's why, the text says, a person alone is afraid. Then it thought: there's nothing here but me.
What am I afraid of? And the fear left.
Because, the text says, fear only comes from a second. Then the self had no joy.
That's why a person alone has no joy. And it wanted a second. Three moods in a few lines: I am, then fear, then longing.
Notice which one thinking can cure. Fear goes the moment the self sees there's nothing else to fear. Loneliness doesn't go that way.
It turns into wanting, and the wanting, tomorrow, becomes a whole world. Later Hindu philosophy uses this little word, aham, in two very different ways.
Ahamkara, the I-maker, is the ego that says me, mine, my name.
And in Advaita Vedanta, the phrase aham brahma asmi, I am Brahman, from a few lines later in this same chapter, points at an I with no name tacked on after it.
The first words in this story come before either one: just I am, and only then the names the ego collects.

how: Students of the Upanishads read this passage as part of the Brihadaranyaka's creation account; in Vedanta teaching it is often paired with aham brahma asmi, I am Brahman, from the same chapter (1.4.10), one of the great sayings.

o: the ego boasting of its own name
a prayer said aloud when knocking on a door
the self's first words, before any name

games.q: the self's first moments — tap the pairs.
p: why we say it before our name

s: the self's very first words in this story are "I am"
aham asmi. so, the text says, it came to be called I.
the self's fear goes away when a second being appears
it goes when the self sees there's nothing but itself: fear comes from a second.
the text explains why people say "it's me" before their name
it traces the habit back to the self's first words.

games.q: you are the self at the very beginning. you look around and there is nothing but you, and you're afraid. what do you do?
o: make something else to keep you company.
ask: there's nothing here but me, so what am I afraid of?
games.why: the self reasons it through, and the fear leaves: fear only comes from a second. the loneliness, though, stays, and that's what makes it want a second.

practice: Let the breath settle, and notice the plain sense that you're here: not your name, not your job, not whose child or parent you are. Just: I am.
If a worry comes, ask it gently, as the self did in the story, what in this room, right now, there is to be afraid of, and then come back to I am.

wordCard.voice: Aham asmi. I am. In the Brihadaranyaka, the first words the self ever spoke, before there was anything else to speak to.

orig.note: Sanskrit: aham, I + asmi, am. the same aham is inside ahamkara, the I-maker, the ego.

carryVoice: Your line: i am, before the ego adds a name. Tomorrow, the lonely self finds a way to have a second. Day three hundred sixty-three, done.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.2–3 (fear comes from a second; no joy alone)
